{"id": "2:28/q25", "question": "Does the rebuke imply human creation of disbelief or divine determination?", "turns_on": "How divine causation and human blame fit together.", "positions": [{"id": "2:28/q25/p1", "position": "People produce their disbelief; God does not create or intend it.", "reasons": "Tabarsi infers ownership of the act from its attribution. Razi reports Mu'tazilite arguments: God-created unbelief would make rebuke and command incoherent like blame for illness; they cite 84:20 and 74:49. Other objections cite blame of Satan, Pharaoh and the Samaritan and prayers for protection."}, {"id": "2:28/q25/p2", "position": "Foreknowledge and a divine determinant can necessitate acts without voiding rebuke.", "reasons": "Razi argues foreknowledge makes its contrary impossible; a capacity for both outcomes still needs a determinant, and a servant-supplied one regresses. He mentions both compulsion and human acquisition."}]}
{"id": "2:28/q26", "question": "Are life and death divine favors?", "turns_on": "Whether death and worldly life count as gifts for every addressee.", "positions": [{"id": "2:28/q26/p1", "position": "Life and the whole sequence are gifts calling for gratitude.", "reasons": "Razi compares duty to a nurturing parent; Jishumi insists worldly gifts to unbelievers remain gifts. {"id": "2:28/q27", "question": "What practical warning follows?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:28/q27/p1", "position": "Remember mortality, repent, worship and prepare for judgment.", "reasons": "Tabari urges repentance; Razi depicts grave loneliness and Yaḥyā ibn Mu'ādh's plea for mercy. {"id": "2:28/q28", "question": "How does the verse connect with its surah and nearby verses?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:28/q28/p1", "position": "It resumes the worship call and creation argument.", "reasons": "Biqai links 2:21–22 to creation and prohibition of partners; Ibn Ashur says it returns to 2:21 after 2:25–27 and prepares 2:29, rejecting a local shift from 2:26. Tabatabai sees a second return to the opening call; Elmalili relates earth and heaven as habitation."}, {"id": "2:28/q28/p2", "position": "Parallel verses trace the life-and-return pattern.", "reasons": "Burhan lists amwatan in 3:169 and 77:26 and other formula variants. Ibn Kathir invokes 45:26; Tabatabai compares 32:7–11, 23:14 and 20:55."}, {"id": "2:28/q28/p3", "position": "The Adam account warns and verifies prophethood.", "reasons": "Tabari says Adam and Iblis show repentance and pride, while Muhammad's inaccessible scriptural knowledge evidences mission; Muqatil says polytheists objected to resurrection after dust, prompting the next verse."}, {"id": "2:28/q28/p4", "position": "The account includes human reason and nature only insofar as they bear on guidance.", "reasons": "Tabatabai says the Quran selects journey details for guidance, happiness and misery, while human intellect and the subjection of creation frame the account."}, {"id": "2:28/q28/p5", "position": "A later return verse, 2:281, is reported as last revealed.", "reasons": "Biqai describes 2:281 as the final comprehensive address to those facing judgment."}]}
{"id": "2:28/q29", "question": "What inward states do death and life represent?", "turns_on": "Which inward condition each temporal stage symbolizes.", "positions": [{"id": "2:28/q29/p1", "position": "Shirk or ignorance gives way to tawhid or knowledge.", "reasons": "Sulami and Abu Hayyan transmit movement from association to unity, ignorance to knowledge and discord to harmony; Qashani calls disbelief veiling."}, {"id": "2:28/q29/p2", "position": "Ego-life dies and heart or secrets come alive.", "reasons": "Sulami's Baghdadi and Ibn Ata, Qushayri and Alusi describe ego-death, unveiling and the end of servant traits. Qushayri says realized people alternate subsistence and extinction."}, {"id": "2:28/q29/p3", "position": "Own witnessing dies and divine witnessing begins.", "reasons": "Faris describes successive loss of private witnessing; Qashani speaks of annihilation in unity and abiding through the Real."}, {"id": "2:28/q29/p4", "position": "Distance from God is death and being through Him life.", "reasons": "Al-Shibli's reading appears in Sulami and Abu Hayyan."}, {"id": "2:28/q29/p5", "position": "The rebuke is strongest because inert things do not contest God.", "reasons": "Al-Wasiti locates opposition in spiritual forms."}]}
{"id": "2:28/q30", "question": "How is inward return understood?", "turns_on": "Whether final inward return is witnessing, grasp, or ascent.", "positions": [{"id": "2:28/q30/p1", "position": "Return from personal witnessing to God and His sacred law.", "reasons": "Faris describes total return; Qushayri describes enactment through the Real and the servant in God's grasp."}, {"id": "2:28/q30/p2", "position": "Witnessing of attributes or vision of essence.", "reasons": "Qashani distinguishes the two unities."}, {"id": "2:28/q30/p3", "position": "Prophets ascend and saints are drawn.", "reasons": "Najmiyya cites 89:28 and traces hidden existence, spirit formation, sense-bound death, revelation or faith and guidance by law."}]}
{"id": "2:28/q31", "question": "Does the verse allow reincarnation?", "turns_on": "Whether initial dead implies a previous embodied life.", "positions": [{"id": "2:28/q31/p1", "position": "No; the sequence culminates in resurrection and recompense.", "reasons": "Kuran Yolu rejects scriptural, rational and scientific support for repeated embodiment. {"id": "2:28/q32", "question": "What postmortem report is cited?", "turns_on": "Whether death in the cited report is literal.", "positions": [{"id": "2:28/q32/p1", "position": "Sinful believers in the Fire truly die, then revive after intercession.", "reasons": "Qurtubi cites Muslim's Abu Sa'id report: they become charcoal, then grow by Paradise's rivers like flood-borne seeds. {"id": "2:28/q33", "question": "How is the rhetorical force of wonder classified?", "turns_on": "Which rhetorical category explains the question.", "positions": [{"id": "2:28/q33/p1", "position": "Wonder is a secondary force of question or report.", "reasons": "Burhan and Itqan discuss taxonomies of two through ten speech kinds; Akhfash lists six. {"id": "2:28/q34", "question": "What larger human journey does the verse describe?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:28/q34/p1", "position": "Human dependence leads to accountability and different final outcomes.", "reasons": "Elmalili says people cannot own or remake life and are judged by acquired deeds under 99:7–8. Tabatabai traces material origin to creative command and distinguishes happiness rising from misery descending; Biqai says voluntary return through knowledge precedes compelled return."}, {"id": "2:28/q34/p2", "position": "Mortality counters attachment to worldly pleasure.", "reasons": "Razi pictures possessions and body abandoned in the grave with 23:100; Elmalili recommends lawful gratitude and sincerity."}]}
{"id": "2:29/q01", "question": "Who does the opening 'He' identify?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:29/q01/p1", "position": "God, the creator and knower named in the preceding verse.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī links the pronoun to God in 2:28; Biqāʿī's al-Ḥarālī sees the unseen sustaining essence disclosed by His names."}]}
{"id": "2:29/q02", "question": "How is huwa read in inward remembrance?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:29/q02/p1", "position": "It indicates God's unique unseen essence and becomes a center of repeated remembrance.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports people of God treating huwa as a divine name. Spiritual elders repeat the name with every breath while its referent eludes analogy."}]}

{"id": "2:29/q05", "question": "What does khalq mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether khalq designates actual origination or prior determination in this context.", "positions": [{"id": "2:29/q05/p1", "position": "God originated the thing after nonexistence.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Qurṭubī define divine creation as bringing it into existence; Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Qurṭubī contrast human making after initial composition and cite poetic usage."}, {"id": "2:29/q05/p2", "position": "Khalq can mean determining or measuring a thing.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī gives this lexical sense; al-Ālūsī uses determination or divine intention as one solution to the creation-order difficulty."}]}
{"id": "2:29/q06", "question": "How is khalaqa read?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:29/q06/p1", "position": "The standard reading is Form I perfect active khalaqa.", "reasons": "Qirāʾāt-ER states the standard vocalization."}]}
{"id": "2:29/q07", "question": "What does the verse mean by creating earthly things 'for you'?", "turns_on": "Whether the lām names practical benefit, religious evidence, general gift, or the human vocation behind those gifts.", "positions": [{"id": "2:29/q07/p1", "position": "They serve human worldly use and religious reflection.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī includes livelihood, obedience and proofs of oneness; al-Wāḥidī distinguishes use from reflection and says even harmful beasts deter sin. Rāzī lists animals, plants, minerals, mountains and crafts; Abū Ḥayyān adds food, clothing, marriage, transport and scenery. Al-Bayḍāwī includes images of afterlife joy and pain; Ibn ʿĀshūr stresses changing times and the visible kinds. Ṭabāṭabāʾī reads the heaven's making as part of the favor to humanity."}, {"id": "2:29/q07/p2", "position": "Its primary benefit is reflection and proof of divine oneness and resurrection.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Qurṭubī appeal to the surrounding life, death and heaven signs; al-Qurṭubī adds that snakes and scorpions can warn of punishment. Al-Jishumī's al-Aṣamm uses seven heavens from smoke as a resurrection proof; al-Wāḥidī says direct sight of danger affects the heart more than a report."}, {"id": "2:29/q07/p3", "position": "The things were subjected as a favor, provision and blessing to humanity.", "reasons": "Qatāda repeatedly explains subjection for Adam's children; al-Ṭabarī emphasizes favor and evidence; Biqāʿī says every earthly element supports the rest."}, {"id": "2:29/q07/p4", "position": "The cosmos is for humanity so that humanity may wholly serve God.", "reasons": "Al-Sulamī's Ibn ʿAṭāʾ and Bursevī's inward source urge detachment from possessions; Elmalılı cites 51:56 for worship as the human end."}]}
{"id": "2:29/q08", "question": "What is included in 'what is on earth'?", "turns_on": "Whether earth denotes the physical globe and its contents or the entire lower region.", "positions": [{"id": "2:29/q08/p1", "position": "The earthly contents, such as animals, plants, minerals and all useful products.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr describes the land-and-sea globe and says its container's creation is implied. Bursevī takes the things contained; al-Wāḥidī and Elmalılı allow some things to harm some individuals. Abū Ḥayyān links this with 2:22's earlier gift of earth as a resting place."}, {"id": "2:29/q08/p2", "position": "The lower realm, including earth itself and everything below the upper realm.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Bayḍāwī allow earth to mean the lower regions; al-Ālūsī also invokes the encompassing Throne or conceptual direction. Abū Ḥayyān finds this distant from the phrase's literal scope, and Ibn ʿĀshūr says earth literally names the globe."}, {"id": "2:29/q08/p3", "position": "The clause covers whatever people need.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī reports this narrower explanation."}]}

{"id": "2:29/q10", "question": "What does the lām in 'for you' express?", "turns_on": "Which function of the Arabic lām fits the context.", "positions": [{"id": "2:29/q10/p1", "position": "Purpose, cause, and benefit: for your sake.", "reasons": "Ibn Kaysān glosses it min ajlikum; Abū Ḥayyān prefers benefit. {"id": "2:29/q11", "question": "Does the verse establish original permissibility or ownership?", "turns_on": "Whether a statement of human benefit is also a legal grant, what reason can establish before revelation, and whether a collective grant entails individual ownership.", "positions": [{"id": "2:29/q11/p1", "position": "Useful things are presumptively permissible unless evidence forbids them.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf and jurists infer permission from creation for benefit; al-Ṭabrisī requires proof for exclusive control. Al-Bayḍāwī distinguishes collective grant from every individual's ownership. Elmalılı grounds permission in revealed text rather than reason."}, {"id": "2:29/q11/p2", "position": "Things are originally forbidden until authorization.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says most proponents except necessities such as breathing and motion; Abū Ḥayyān states their principle that one should not act without leave."}, {"id": "2:29/q11/p3", "position": "Judgment is suspended before revelation.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya prefers suspension for a genuinely novel case; Abū al-Ḥasan and most Mālikīs say reason creates no ruling. Ibn al-Ṣāʾigh replies that cases always have a text, precedent or continuing default. Ibn ʿĀshūr distinguishes post-revelation harms from benefits."}, {"id": "2:29/q11/p4", "position": "The verse grants no legal default; it gives proof of God's power and favor.", "reasons": "Ibn al-ʿArabī and Ibn ʿĀshūr read the address as reminder to disbelievers, not legislation. Al-Qurṭubī argues that benefit need not require tasting and some goods are lethal. Abū Ḥayyān notes the lām is equivocal."}, {"id": "2:29/q11/p5", "position": "All things are common to everyone, with no exclusive private claim.", "reasons": "Rāzī reports permissivists; Rāzī, al-Ālūsī and Ibn ʿĀshūr answer that a grant to humanity collectively can be distributed to individuals under separate proof."}, {"id": "2:29/q11/p6", "position": "Eating clay is forbidden because it is earth itself, not what is in earth.", "reasons": "Rāzī answers that minerals and veins lie within earth and mention of contents does not exclude earth; Abū Ḥayyān also reports this inference."}, {"id": "2:29/q11/p7", "position": "Unrestricted permission cancels duties and prohibitions for realized lovers.", "reasons": "Bursevī attributes this to libertine Sufis and rejects it as contradicting revealed commands and prohibitions."}]}

{"id": "2:29/q15", "question": "What does thumma mark between the earth and heaven clauses?", "turns_on": "Whether the conjunction orders events, ranks the greater act, or structures the recital.", "positions": [{"id": "2:29/q15/p1", "position": "A higher rank or a new stage in the discourse, not necessarily later time.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī cites 90:17; al-Bayḍāwī and Biqāʿī stress heaven's greater rank. Ibn ʿĀshūr says one subject linked by thumma can carry imagined delay in rank, while Elmalılı traces order of human awareness from self to earth to sky; al-Qāshānī marks the difference of realms."}, {"id": "2:29/q15/p2", "position": "It marks temporal succession, perhaps with intervening earth preparation.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān says this is the ordinary force; one account allows an interval for mountains and provisions in 41:9–10. {"id": "2:29/q16", "question": "Which came first, earth or heaven, and how are the creation verses reconciled?", "turns_on": "Whether khalq and spreading are distinct events, whether the sky existed as smoke before its sevenfold shaping, and how strictly thumma and baʿda convey temporal order.", "positions": [{"id": "2:29/q16/p1", "position": "Earth's body was created first; heaven was fashioned next; earth was spread and furnished afterward.", "reasons": "Mujāhid, Ibn ʿAbbās and most early exegetes reconcile 2:29 and 41:9–12 with 79:30 by separating creation from spreading. Ibn Kathīr likens construction to foundations rising upward; Ibn ʿĀshūr mentions geological cooling and crust movement. Rāzī objects that a body cannot exist unspread and contents require spread earth; al-Ālūsī replies it began small and its contents existed as materials."}, {"id": "2:29/q16/p2", "position": "Heaven or its vapor preceded earth; the sky was later fashioned into seven.", "reasons": "Qatāda, Muqātil and al-Suddī are reported for heaven first. Al-Qurṭubī prefers primordial vapor, then earth, then fashioned heaven, then spreading; Ibn ʿĀshūr favors heaven first because 79:30 is stronger for sequence, with astronomy and Genesis as further support. Al-Ālūsī says investigators regard visible earthly contents as later. Al-Qurṭubī prefers the account with primordial vapor before earth, despite an Ibn ʿAbbās variant reversing the order, and says speculation cannot decide it."}, {"id": "2:29/q16/p3", "position": "The earth-first wording names divine determination or initial material, while heaven's actual form came before earthly contents.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī uses khalq as determination or intention, cites 41:11's command to heaven and earth, and reads towns and provisions as matter and origins; the order of each sūra fits its theme."}, {"id": "2:29/q16/p4", "position": "The textual order is rhetorical, so it need not establish chronological earth-first creation.", "reasons": "Rāzī prefers enumerating blessings; al-Ṭabrisī and Ibn Kathīr report discourse-order resolutions. Elmalılı traces human perception and allows a narrower chronological sense in which the earth's separate body affects later heavenly ordering."}, {"id": "2:29/q16/p5", "position": "The question remains difficult because cited verses appear to order the events differently.", "reasons": "Rāzī sets out the apparent clash of 2:29, 41:9–10 and 79:27–30; Abū Ḥayyān reports both camps; al-Ālūsī says it troubled readers since the Companions."}]}
{"id": "2:29/q17", "question": "What creation-day schedule do the reports give?", "turns_on": "How the six days are allocated, especially the Saturday report's attribution.", "positions": [{"id": "2:29/q17/p1", "position": "Earth Sunday and Monday, provisions and mountains Tuesday and Wednesday, heavens Thursday and Friday; Adam in Friday's last hour.", "reasons": "ʿAbd Allāh b. Salām and reports through Ibn ʿAbbās give six days, with Friday also the hour of Resurrection. Ibn al-Jawzī transmits another allocation of earth and contents over four days then heaven over two."}, {"id": "2:29/q17/p2", "position": "Soil Saturday, mountains Sunday, trees Monday, harmful things Tuesday, light Wednesday, animals Thursday, Adam late Friday.", "reasons": "Abū Hurayra transmits this as Prophetic, but Ibn Kathīr reports ʿAlī b. al-Madīnī, al-Bukhārī and al-Bayhaqī tracing the schedule to Kaʿb and explaining its mistaken elevation to the Prophet."}, {"id": "2:29/q17/p3", "position": "The earth and its provisions took four days and the heavens two, totaling six.", "reasons": "Rāzī bases this on 41:9–10; the al-Suddī narrative names Tuesday and Wednesday for mountains and plants."}]}
{"id": "2:29/q18", "question": "From what substance did heaven and earth arise according to the reports?", "turns_on": "Which reported primordial material and sequence is being followed.", "positions": [{"id": "2:29/q18/p1", "position": "Water under the Throne produced smoke or vapor for heaven and dried into earth, which was divided into seven.", "reasons": "Al-Suddī's multi-Companion report details water, smoke, one earth, seven earths, then seven heavens; Ibn ʿAbbās describes heating water into rising vapor. {"id": "2:29/q19", "question": "What holds the earth steady in the cosmological reports?", "turns_on": "Which reported cosmic support is at issue and how the cited verse about divine sustaining is read.", "positions": [{"id": "2:29/q19/p1", "position": "Earth rests on a fish over layered supports; mountains prevent shaking when the fish moves.", "reasons": "Al-Suddī's account invokes 68:1, 16:15 and 31:16; versions list water, slab, angel, rock and wind. {"id": "2:29/q21", "question": "What other Arabic senses of istawā inform the explanation?", "turns_on": "Which lexical sense the construction with ilā activates.", "positions": [{"id": "2:29/q21/p1", "position": "It can mean reaching maturity, becoming straight or settled, turning toward, rising, or gaining mastery.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ, Ṭabarī and others list these senses; Ṭabarī cites Ṭirimmāḥ's verse for straightening and rejects reading a horse poem as coming toward. {"id": "2:29/q22", "question": "How is istawā pronounced?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:29/q22/p1", "position": "Hijaz speakers use open pronunciation, while Najd speakers incline the final alif by imāla.", "reasons": "Naḥḥās and al-Qurṭubī connect imāla to the yāʾ origin; Abū Ḥayyān says both occur among the seven readers."}]}
{"id": "2:29/q23", "question": "What is al-samāʾ here?", "turns_on": "Whether 'sky' names an upper direction or a preexisting celestial substance, and when it became a fashioned heaven.", "positions": [{"id": "2:29/q23/p1", "position": "The elevated upper realm, direction, canopy, or celestial bodies.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj derives sky from elevation and includes clouds; al-Zamakhsharī and al-Nasafī name upper regions. {"id": "2:29/q24", "question": "Why does a singular 'heaven' lead to plural 'them'?", "turns_on": "Whether al-samāʾ is a generic singular, a morphological plural, a whole with parts, or whether the pronoun awaits explanation.", "positions": [{"id": "2:29/q24/p1", "position": "Al-samāʾ is singular in form but generic or collective in meaning, denoting all heavens.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ, al-Akhfash and the grammarians allow singular wording with a collective sense; al-Wāḥidī cites 26:77 and 26:16 and Qutrub's poetry. {"id": "2:29/q25", "question": "What does sawwāhunna mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the emphasis is on completed ordered creation or on equal/smoothed surfaces.", "positions": [{"id": "2:29/q25/p1", "position": "God perfected, proportioned, ordered or straightened the heavens without defects.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī defines taswiya as preparing and correcting; al-Rabīʿ and Abū al-ʿĀliya call it fashioning and perfecting. {"id": "2:29/q26", "question": "How is 'seven heavens' parsed after sawwāhunna?", "turns_on": "The pronoun's antecedent, the valency of sawwā, and whether the numeral specifies, apposes, or qualifies it.", "positions": [{"id": "2:29/q26/p1", "position": "Sabʿa samāwāt is an apposition to the object pronoun, referring back to heaven.", "reasons": "Muḥammad b. al-Walīd and Abū Ḥayyān allow apposition; al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī prefer it because the numeral is underived and maintains the antecedent link; Elmalılı calls it partitive."}, {"id": "2:29/q26/p2", "position": "It is apposition to an ambiguous pronoun explained by what follows.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn lists this as a weaker alternative because it relies on al-Zamakhsharī's disputed pronoun analysis."}, {"id": "2:29/q26/p3", "position": "Sabʿ is an accusative circumstantial qualifier.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash allows this; Abū Ḥayyān says possible but prospective, and al-Samīn calls it remote."}, {"id": "2:29/q26/p4", "position": "An implied min makes it 'He fashioned seven of them.'", "reasons": "Naḥḥās analogizes the partitive to 7:155; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn object that sawwā does not behave like ikhtāra and the construction implies more than seven."}, {"id": "2:29/q26/p5", "position": "It is a second object with sawwā meaning 'made into.'", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn object that this sense and valency of sawwā are not established."}, {"id": "2:29/q26/p6", "position": "It is an accusative specification explaining the pronoun.", "reasons": "Bursevī and al-Ālūsī list this parse."}]}
{"id": "2:29/q27", "question": "What form and force does the number seven have?", "turns_on": "Whether the numeral is an exact count or a conventional expression of multiplicity.", "positions": [{"id": "2:29/q27/p1", "position": "Sabʿ is the numeral form paired with a feminine counted noun; sabʿa pairs with masculine.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī, al-Jishumī and al-Ṭabrisī discuss the gender forms, with occasional departures; al-Ṭabrisī also associates seven with multiplied strength. Abū Ḥayyān lists seven days, earths, visible planets, seas and Hell gates as major counted things."}, {"id": "2:29/q27/p2", "position": "Seven can conventionally intensify or mean several or many.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān cites Arabic seven and seventy as emphatic multiples, with 17:4 and 9:80; Asad invokes lexicons, and Kur'an Yolu allows many heavens."}]}

{"id": "2:29/q31", "question": "What do reports say about the heavens' names, materials and inhabitants?", "turns_on": "Which transmitted description or name list is being followed.", "positions": [{"id": "2:29/q31/p1", "position": "Salmān assigns seven named materials: green emerald, silver, red ruby, pearl, red gold, yellow ruby and light.", "reasons": "Al-Durr names Raqīʿa, Azqalūn, Qaydūm, Maʿūna, Riqʿa, Daqnā and Arībā; Bursevī repeats the material list."}, {"id": "2:29/q31/p2", "position": "ʿAlī names the lowest Raqī and seventh al-Surākh.", "reasons": "Al-Durr preserves the alternative names."}, {"id": "2:29/q31/p3", "position": "Heaven is a contained wave or is whiter than milk; it was formed from smoke and water.", "reasons": "Abū al-Jald answers Ibn ʿAbbās with the wave description; Kaʿb gives whiteness, and ʿAlī swears to smoke and water. {"id": "2:29/q32", "question": "How many earths are there, and what are they like?", "turns_on": "What 'their like' in 65:12 means and the reliability of specific reports.", "positions": [{"id": "2:29/q32/p1", "position": "There are seven earths corresponding in number to the heavens.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī prefers this reading of 65:12 and adduces reports that a land thief will be encircled by seven earths and that tawḥīd outweighs seven heavens and earths. {"id": "2:29/q33", "question": "What was the first created thing according to these reports?", "turns_on": "The scope of 'first' and whether water, pen, or light and darkness are counted.", "positions": [{"id": "2:29/q33/p1", "position": "Water, or water and other willed things, preceded later creation.", "reasons": "A Prophetic report says everything was created from water; al-Bayhaqī says God created water without prior matter or model. {"id": "2:29/q38", "question": "Why does the verse end with divine knowledge?", "turns_on": "Whether the ending emphasizes the knowledge needed for creation, awareness of the addressees, or preparation for Adam's story.", "positions": [{"id": "2:29/q38/p1", "position": "Precise, faultless creation reveals and requires complete knowledge.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī, al-Ṭabrisī, Rāzī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Ālūsī and Ibn ʿĀshūr reason from ordered work to a knowing maker; al-Biqāʿī and al-Itqān find the ending especially apt. {"id": "2:29/q39", "question": "What theological claims follow from universal creative knowledge?", "turns_on": "How universal knowledge interacts with divine will, human action, and wisdom.", "positions": [{"id": "2:29/q39/p1", "position": "An ordered creator knows particulars; human acts and divine willing cannot be separated from detailed knowledge.", "reasons": "Rāzī uses specification by measure to argue for will and against Muʿtazilite human origination of acts whose details humans do not know; the verse also counters philosophers who deny divine knowledge of particulars."}, {"id": "2:29/q39/p2", "position": "The creator is powerful, knowing, purposeful and deserving of gratitude.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī draws this from creation for even disbelievers; Elmalılı says divine knowledge underlies the prepared fit between causes, effects and human life."}]}

{"id": "2:29/q42", "question": "How does the verse connect to the preceding creation and resurrection argument?", "turns_on": "How the new reminder of cosmic gifts advances the prior rebuke and resurrection proof.", "positions": [{"id": "2:29/q42/p1", "position": "It adds visible cosmic creation and human provision to the prior life, death and resurrection proof.", "reasons": "Muqātil cites 40:57; al-Wāḥidī says creating heaven and earth makes re-creation credible. {"id": "2:29/q45", "question": "What rhetorical details mark the move from earth to heaven?", "turns_on": "What rhetorical work the order and the paired verbs do.", "positions": [{"id": "2:29/q45/p1", "position": "The shift magnifies the higher creation and recalls God's governance over feared events from above.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī and al-Ḥarālī emphasize heaven's beauty, purity and the reassurance that God governs what may descend; Ibn ʿĀshūr calls for renewed attention to the greater sign."}, {"id": "2:29/q45/p2", "position": "Istawā and sawwāhun echo one another in sound while linking divine direction to perfected order.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī calls the correspondence graceful; Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it modified paronomasia."}, {"id": "2:29/q45/p3", "position": "The verse starts with earth because it is nearer human experience.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī and Elmalılı say the tangible earth is the more immediate sign; al-Ālūsī contrasts al-Baqara's human-benefit context with al-Nāziʿāt's display of power."}]}
